Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 ROAD OCC: LEARNING WHEN TO PERSIST, TRANSPORT, OR REFRESH MEMORY FOR ROADSIDE OCCUPANCY PREDICTION Anonymous authors Paper under double-blind review ABSTRACT 3D semantic occupancy prediction has advanced rapidly for ego-centric driving, while camera-only roadside occupancy remains underexplored. Fixed cameras make history valuable for sparse or occluded traffic, but coordinate alignment corrects only sensor geometry and leaves moving-object evidence at stale locations. Flow-based fusion can propose a historical address, yet cannot determine whether the retrieved feature provides supported evidence. We therefore formulate temporal memory as supervised soft routing among evidence sources before fusion. In this work, we present RoadOcc, in which each selected voxel predicts whether to persist rigidly aligned memory, transport memory from a velocity-addressed location, or refresh it with current evidence. Dynamic-Aware Cross-Attention (DCA) locates motion-sensitive candidates, Multi-scale Voxel Velocity Estimation (VVE) estimates their transport addresses, and state-conditioned Velocity-Guided Dynamic Sparse Fusion (VDSF) predicts a three-way source-routing distribution over these candidates. This connected design determines where temporal reasoning is needed, where history should be read, and whether it should be used. On InfraOcc, RoadOcc achieves 65.29 mIoU and 32.37 dynamic mIoU, outperforming STCOcc by 4.44 and 4.71 points, respectively, while reducing Direct MAVE from 1.946 to 1.669. Controlled transfer and component ablations further support the routing design. Additional implementation and evaluation details are provided in the supplementary material. 1 INTRODUCTION Semantic occupancy prediction reconstructs free space, static layout, and traffic participants in a common voxel volume. Camera-only methods have made this representation practical through sparse voxel queries, BEV lifting, tri-plane features, and unified panoptic volumes (Cao & de Charette, 2022; Li et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a). However, these methods are predominantly developed for moving platforms, where each observation is interpreted in an ego-centric frame. A roadside sensor instead repeatedly observes the same scene, producing a persistent scaffold overlaid by sparse, short-lived dynamic events. This makes temporal memory valuable but turns physically correct reuse into a central challenge. The same history can provide either valid support or stale evidence. Rigidly aligned memory preserves static layout and can recover weak or occluded vehicle boundaries, but it does not relocate an object that moved within the fixed coordinate system. Reading such memory from the former footprint can blur a dynamic boundary, duplicate an object, or attach it to nearby static layout. Discarding history avoids these errors but also removes useful support. The challenge is therefore not simply whether to use history, but which form of history is valid at each location. Recent temporal methods demonstrate the value of multi-frame context for occupancy, flow, and 3D perception (Ma et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Liao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Huang & Huang, 2022; Chang et al., 2024; Leng et al., 2025). Existing designs already incorporate temporal memory, motion alignment, and adaptive fusion. However, they largely formulate history as a retrieved feature whose confidence is adjusted after alignment. This leaves one unresolved question: whether the feature at a flow-proposed address actually supports the current voxel. A stationary object may reuse rigid memory, a moving object may retrieve memory near \(\mathbf{x} - \Delta t\,\mathbf{v}_t(\mathbf{x})\), and an appearing, occluded, or historically unsupported object must instead rely on current evidence. Continuous feature weighting can represent these alternatives, but existing formulations typically lack a direct training signal for when transported history must be rejected. We therefore formulate temporal occupancy as supervised evidence-source routing. *Should each selected voxel Persist, Transport, or Refresh?* Persist reads the rigidly aligned address, Transport reads a velocity-compensated address, and Refresh uses current image evidence. The core principle is not to make flow “stronger”: flow supplies a candidate source address, whereas P/T/R decides whether rigid history, transported history, or no history is admissible for the current voxel. This decision is directly supervisable and exposes which source supports each prediction. ![Figure showing current cameras, camera FOV, occupancy flow, current OCC, past OCC, and P/T/R target for real-scene evidence routing](page_1_400_239_420_312.png) Figure 1: **Real-scene evidence for explicit source routing.** The top row shows current views, camera FOVs, and current-aligned occupancy flow (a–c). The bottom row shows current/past occupancy and P/T/R targets (d–f), illustrating a persistent bus, transported car, and newly visible cars assigned Refresh. We instantiate this principle in RoadOcc as a staged routing process. Dynamic-Aware Cross-Attention (DCA) first uses current semantics to identify the voxels that require temporal reasoning. Restricted to these candidates, Multi-scale Voxel Velocity Estimation (VVE) estimates where their historical support should be retrieved. State-Conditioned Velocity-Guided Dynamic Sparse Fusion (VDSF) then uses the resulting addresses to predict a soft distribution over rigid memory, transported memory, and current evidence. Because each stage resolves the uncertainty required by the next, the temporal source choice becomes explicit and trainable. Source-aligned P/T/R targets and a multi-scale route objective provide direct supervision for the entire chain. Our evaluation tests the same mechanism rather than treating velocity as an isolated auxiliary task. The InfraOcc benchmark measures predictive accuracy, while dynamic-first temporal diagnostics test whether gains coincide with improved support coverage without sacrificing static accuracy. Figure 1 grounds the three evidence-source alternatives in one real roadside sequence. Our contributions are summarized below. * We propose RoadOcc, which formulates roadside temporal occupancy as Persist–Transport–Refresh routing issue. The router decides whether a flow-proposed historical source is admissible, separating reuse history from evidence that must be relocated or discarded. * We realize this principle through a staged DCA–VVE–VDSF chain. DCA selects where temporal reasoning is needed, enabling VVE to estimate motion-compensated historical addresses that VDSF uses to softly route rigid, transported, or current evidence. * We evaluate the source-routing hypothesis with dynamic-first occupancy, flow-advected next-frame consistency, velocity, and support-recall diagnostics. Controlled ablations isolate address estimation from the decision to adopt or refresh historical evidence. ## 2 Related Work ### 2.1 Camera Occupancy and Roadside Perception Camera occupancy methods lift multi-view image evidence into volumetric representations. MonoScene Cao & de Charette (2022) and VoxFormer Li et al. (2023a) establish image- Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 based semantic scene completion, while BEVDet, BEVDepth, and BEVFormer improve multi-view lifting and BEV reasoning (Huang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023b; 2025b). Occupancy-specific designs span tri-plane, dense, sparse, Gaussian, and forward-backward representations (Huang et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2023c), as well as panoptic and instance-aware prediction (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a). Unlike MC-BEVRO’s roadside BEV occupancy monitoring (Vaghela et al., 2025), RoadOcc routes evidence for class-aware 3D occupancy. InfraOcc provides a roadside occupancy benchmark emphasizing persistent infrastructure (Yang et al., 2026). Figure 2 reveals its temporal asymmetry. Fixed roadway structure provides broad, stable support, while dynamic participants form sparse, short-lived trails. This asymmetry favors retaining static context while selectively relocating moving evidence. ![Three-panel figure showing static semantic persistence, dynamic transience, and occupied-frame percentage curves for InfraOcc.](page_1_400_259_405_207.png) Figure 2: **Static-to-dynamic persistence in InfraOcc.** ## 2.2 Temporal Occupancy, Motion, and Alignment Temporal occupancy methods maintain or forecast scene state, sometimes jointly with flow. Cam4DOcc, OccWorld, UniOcc, ALOcc, STCOcc, and Let Occ Flow model dynamics alongside volumetric semantics (Ma et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Liao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2026). ST-Occ conditions memory on uncertainty and dynamics, while GDFusion organizes scene, motion-calibration, and geometric cues for temporal fusion (Leng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b). Recurrent BEV models also maintain aligned memory (Huang & Huang, 2022; Chang et al., 2024), while SelfOcc and ForecastOcc learn from video or predict future occupancy (Huang et al., 2024a; Mohan et al., 2026). These methods establish motion-aware alignment and adaptive fusion. RoadOcc focuses on the subsequent source-validity decision by directly supervising a mutually exclusive choice among rigid history, transported history, and current evidence. Its next-frame score evaluates the resulting motion field rather than a forecasting head. This speed-dependent gap favors selective motion compensation over a uniform temporal warp. # 3 Method ## 3.1 Preliminary Analysis Let $\mathcal{I}_t = \{ I^n_t \}_{n=1}^{4}$ denote the synchronized roadside images at time $t$. RoadOcc predicts semantic occupancy $y_t$ over a voxel domain $\Omega$ and a planar velocity field $v_t : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$. Among the 18 occu- 3 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 ![Figure with eight panels showing RoadOcc execution trace: predicted occupancy, ground-truth occupancy, DCA candidates, VVE flow, and routed voxel categories Persist, Transport, Refresh, and PTR-routed voxels](page_226_132_546_273.png) Figure 4: **RoadOcc execution trace.** Current occupancy evidence identifies DCA candidates (a–c), VVE estimates their motion-aware historical addresses (d), and VDSF separates routed voxels into Persist, Transport, and Refresh evidence (e–h). pancy states, the dynamic set is \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{dyn}}=\{\text{bicycle, bus, car, motorcycle, pedestrian, truck}\}\). Velocity is expressed in the common roadside horizontal frame. Rigid alignment removes camera motion but not object motion. Under a locally constant velocity approximation, history supporting a current voxel \(\mathbf{x}\) is read from \[ \bar{\mathbf{h}}_{t-\Delta t}(\mathbf{x})=\mathrm{Sample}\left(\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{t-\Delta t}, \mathbf{x}-\Delta t\,\mathbf{v}_t(\mathbf{x})\right), \tag{1} \] where \(\bar{\mathbf{h}}\) is rigidly aligned history and Sample is trilinear interpolation. The three candidates are rigid history at \(\mathbf{x}\) (Persist), flow-addressed history at \(\mathbf{x}-\Delta t\,\mathbf{v}_t(\mathbf{x})\) (Transport), and current evidence (Refresh). Equation 1 specifies only an address. VDSF still decides whether the sampled source has class-consistent historical support. ### 3.2 Overview RoadOcc decodes \(\{V_t^s\}_{s\in\{1/8,1/4,1/2\}}\) from coarse to fine. At each scale, DCA revisits motion-sensitive image evidence, VVE proposes its historical address, and VDSF routes rigid, transported, or current evidence. Estimating the address before source admissibility lets VDSF reject unsupported memory. The fused state is upsampled to the next scale, yielding full-resolution occupancy and velocity. Figures 4 and 5 show this sequence and its progressive output. ### 3.3 Dynamic-Aware Cross-Attention (DCA) Dynamic objects occupy few voxels, so uniformly repeating image cross-attention spends most computation on stable structure. DCA instead derives a candidate map after the first nonempty-guided image update. Let \(\pi_{t,\mathrm{cur}}^s\) and \(\pi_{t,\mathrm{sta}}^s\) denote the provisional distributions produced by the current and static prediction heads after the first image update, and let \(C_{t,\mathrm{sta}}^+\) contain the static classes and free space. DCA uses two complementary cues. The first is the mean semantic discrepancy \(\delta_{t,\mathrm{sta}}^s\) between the two distributions over \(C_{t,\mathrm{sta}}^+\). The second is the current dynamic probability \(p_{t,\mathrm{dyn}}^s\). Their normalized maximum forms the candidate map \[ c_t^s(\mathbf{x})=\mathrm{Norm}\left(\max\{\delta_{t,\mathrm{sta}}^s(\mathbf{x}), p_{t,\mathrm{dyn}}^s(\mathbf{x})\}\right). \tag{2} \] Here Norm divides by the spatial maximum within each sample, with the denominator clamped to \(10^{-6}\). The discrepancy cue recovers locations whose current evidence departs from the static hypothesis, while the direct cue retains already visible actors. Taking their maximum is important because an early semantic miss can still be recovered from change evidence instead of being removed from subsequent reasoning. The candidate map controls a second image cross-attention rather than directly reweighting the voxel feature. Following projected deformable attention (Li et al., 2025b) and occupancy-aware reference 4 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 sampling (Liao et al., 2025), let \(\mathbf{q}_{t,x}^{s}\) be the BEV query at \(x\), \(\mathcal{R}_n(\mathbf{x})\) its visible height anchors in camera \(n\), and \(\mathbf{F}_{t}^{n}\) the corresponding image feature. DCA retains \(\mathcal{R}_{n,c}^{s}(\mathbf{x})=\{r\in\mathcal{R}_n(\mathbf{x}):u_r \epsilon \wedge \mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf{x} - \Delta t\,\mathbf{v}_t(\mathbf{x})), \\ R, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \tag{7} \] where Supp tests same-class occupancy at the same height within the local correspondence radius. We use \(\epsilon = 10^{-3}\) m/s and a one-voxel radius to absorb discretization error. The construction follows the semantic occupancy label space used by InfraOcc and is evaluated at every execution scale using its physical cell size, with a native-grid endpoint for full-resolution supervision. Under this rule, supported stationary voxels Persist, supported moving voxels Transport, and voxels without a supported historical candidate Refresh. The supplement specifies the source-alignment and label-generation procedure. At each decoder scale, a shared controller combines the current feature, nearest rigidly aligned history, normalized VVE flow, and upsampled coarser P/T/R distribution. It predicts stage-local logits; a lightweight native head upsamples the finest context with full-resolution flow. Softmax gives \(\alpha_t^s = (\alpha_P, \alpha_T, \alpha_R)\) and the routed candidate \[ \mathbf{h}_t^{\mathrm{PTR}} = \alpha_P \mathbf{h}^P + \alpha_T \mathbf{h}^T + \alpha_R \mathbf{h}^R, \qquad (\alpha_P, \alpha_T, \alpha_R) = \mathrm{softmax}(\psi(\cdot)). \tag{8} \] P/T/R therefore compete as one route distribution rather than independent weights. Fusion uses the soft probabilities; argmax is reserved for diagnostics. Transport is emphasized only when supported, while conflicting history can fall back to Refresh. Let \(\mathbf{H}_t^{\mathrm{PTR},s}(\mathbf{x})\) concatenate the routed candidates from all valid FIFO slots at scale \(s\). VDSF fuses the temporal stack with the current token and its semantic embedding through a channel MLP \[ \mathbf{q}_{t,\mathrm{fuse}}^s(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{q}_t^s(\mathbf{x}) + \Phi_s\left( \left[ \mathbf{q}_t^s(\mathbf{x}),\, \mathbf{H}_t^{\mathrm{PTR},s}(\mathbf{x}),\, \mathrm{Emb}(\pi_t^s(\mathbf{x})) \right] \right). \tag{9} \] The residual is scattered to \(\mathcal{X}_t^s\) and joined with the background path. The fused volume and VVE prior update the stage-local queue. Queue lengths, token budgets, source matching, and routing settings appear in supplementary Secs. 3-5. ### 3.6 Training Objective Training jointly optimizes four functional objectives. \[ \mathcal{L} = \lambda_{\mathrm{depth}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}} + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{mot}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mot}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{route}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{route}}. \tag{10} \] \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}}\) supervises the image view transform with camera-depth targets. \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sem}}\) groups full-resolution and multi-scale semantic occupancy losses together with the static/dynamic and DCA-candidate 6 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027

Scale-wise weights and schedules appear in supplementary Sec. 3. 4 Experiments **Dataset and metrics.** We evaluate camera-only roadside occupancy on InfraOcc, derived from V2X-Real (Xiang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026). Four synchronized views are mapped to 18 occupancy states. Under the InfraOcc protocol, semantic mIoU excludes construction vehicle, trailer, other flat, and Free. Free IoU is reported separately in the class-wise table. We report semantic and geometric IoU, next-frame dynamic IoU, and motion coverage. Direct MAVE covers all GT dynamic voxels, while TP-MAVE conditions on semantic matches and is paired with recall (DSR). InfraOcc is a concurrent dense fixed-roadside occupancy benchmark; because existing roadside datasets mainly provide object-level labels, we use its camera-only protocol and assess generality through matched transfer and controlled studies, with full benchmark details in the supplement. **Implementation details.** RoadOcc uses a ResNet-50 backbone, 256 × 704 images, and three voxel stages from 0.8 m to 0.4 m over $[-64, 64] \times [-64, 64] \times [-4.8, 1.6]$ m. Frames are 0.5 s apart. AdamW training runs for 24 epochs from $5 \times 10^{-4}$ with $10^{-2}$ weight decay and cosine annealing. Comparisons share the voxel range, ignored classes, and evaluator. The $-S$ suffix disables temporal history while retaining the task architecture and training protocol, whereas unmarked temporal variants use their corresponding memory path. Controlled variants keep the backbone, data split, optimizer, schedule, queue reset, and sparse-token configuration fixed unless their designated factor changes. Exact metric, queue, selection, and routing contracts appear in the supplement. The score is the same-class hit rate within the one-voxel matching radius. ## 4.1 Main Results **InfraOcc occupancy benchmark.** Table 2 tests whether the proposed routing design improves occupancy under the InfraOcc evaluator. RoadOcc achieves the strongest result in Table 2 and establishes a new state of the art at 65.29 mIoU, a +4.44 gain over STCOcc. Dynamic mIoU rises by +4.71 to 32.37, while static mIoU rises by +4.24 to 89.98. The joint gain matches the proposed routing mechanism. VVE relocates evidence for moving participants, while P/T/R restricts reuse to supported history. The class-wise results therefore show stronger transient recovery without sacrificing the persistent roadside structure. **Joint occupancy–velocity behavior.** Table 3 tests whether these occupancy gains follow the expected routing mechanism. Direct MAVE measures the quality of the VVE address, and DSR measures the dynamic support retained by P/T/R. Relative to STCOcc, RoadOcc lowers Direct MAVE from 1.946 to 1.669 and raises DSR from 57.12 to 61.11. Adding VDSF P/T/R to CRT-Fusion and STCOcc also raises Dyn. by +1.28 and +1.14, respectively, while improving Direct MAVE and DSR. The matching changes show that VDSF P/T/R generalizes to two flow-aware occupancy backbones, linking the occupancy gain to better address correction and source selection. TP-MAVE conditions on correctly matched semantics and must therefore be read with DSR. Its increase on CRT-Fusion accompanies a +1.89 DSR gain, exposing the coverage–conditional-error trade-off rather than conflating a lower conditional error with broader dynamic recovery. ## 4.2 Ablation Studies Using a shared backbone and (Liao et al., 2025) as the baseline, we sequentially ablate RoadOcc’s decision chain. DCA selects where temporal evidence is needed, VVE locates its historical source, and P/T/R assesses source admissibility. This staged design separates their contributions from generic temporal fusion. Route-wise diagnostics appear in the supplement. **Overall ablation.** Table 4 follows the routing chain. VDSF alone adds only 0.20 mIoU because selecting history without first resolving its location leaves moving evidence misaligned. DCA and VDSF then raise Dyn. by +1.55 and Nxt. by +1.80, showing that current evidence identifies where sparse temporal fusion is useful. **P/T/R source-admissibility supervision.** P/T/R supervises semantic source validity rather than instance correspondence. Persist and Transport require same-class, height-consistent support at the rigid and VVE-addressed locations, while Refresh covers neither source. GT-conditioned diagnostics isolate routing from detection, whereas Dyn., Nxt., Direct MAVE, and DSR retain end-to-end evaluation. The supplement details the target construction. **Visual analysis.** Figure 6 compares zero-motion reading with VVE backtracing. Red-to-green changes show displaced targets recovering same-class history. Because queried targets are fixed, the comparison isolates VVE address quality from the subsequent routing decision. On identical GT dynamic support, Figure 7 shows Persist following aligned support, Transport following displacement, and Refresh rejecting history. Fixing support isolates source choice from detection. This view complements the address control in Figure 6. ![Predicted P/T/R on GT dynamic support showing GT occupancy, predicted occupancy, GT occupancy flow, fused BEV feature, and predicted Persist, Transport, Refresh, and GT P/T/R maps](page_383_624_435_215.png) Figure 7: **Predicted P/T/R on GT dynamic support.** Together, the two visualizations summarize RoadOcc’s evidence-routing principle. VVE resolves *where* each queried voxel should retrieve historical evidence, while P/T/R verifies its semantic validity, preserving supported history and refreshing unreliable evidence before VDSF fusion. ## 5 Conclusion In this work, we present RoadOcc, a voxel-level evidence-source routing framework for temporal roadside occupancy. Rather than relying on implicit temporal aggregation, RoadOcc explicitly determines where supported history should be retrieved and whether it should be reused. DCA uses current image evidence to identify motion-sensitive voxels, VVE estimates their historical source addresses, and VDSF turns these addresses into Persist, Transport, or Refresh decisions. On the reported InfraOcc protocol, the unified formulation achieves state-of-the-art occupancy accuracy while improving dynamic recovery and velocity estimation. A ROADSIDE SENSOR CONFIGURATION InfraOcc reorganizes synchronized V2X-Real streams from object-level cooperative perception into dense roadside occupancy supervision (Yang et al., 2026). Two fixed infrastructure units each carry one LiDAR and two high-resolution cameras under GPS time synchronization. Calibration maps the four camera streams, two point clouds, and occupancy annotations into a common roadside coordinate system. The four cameras are the only exteroceptive model inputs. LiDAR is used solely for benchmark construction and ground-truth generation. Thus the reported setting remains camera-only despite the multimodal data-collection platform. ![Infrastructure-side sensor configuration showing two fixed infrastructure units, LiDAR point clouds, and four synchronized camera views calibrated to a common roadside frame.](page_1_496_385_323_218.png) Figure A1: Infrastructure-side sensor configuration. Two fixed units provide four synchronized cameras and two LiDARs calibrated to a common roadside frame. Roadside benchmarks such as Rope3D and DAIR-V2X also study fixed or cooperative perception (Ye et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022), but primarily evaluate object-level detection. InfraOcc instead retains a fixed coordinate system for dense occupancy, exposing voxel-level persistence and displacement. This property is essential for testing whether a current voxel retrieves its historical feature from a source-consistent location. A.1 BENCHMARK SCOPE AND CONSTRUCTION CONTRACT InfraOcc is a concurrent benchmark derived from V2X-Real. We are unaware of a second real-world benchmark that simultaneously provides fixed roadside sensing, temporally continuous dense semantic voxel labels, and a compatible camera-only evaluation protocol. Ego-centric occupancy benchmarks assume a moving sensor frame, while existing roadside and cooperative datasets predominantly expose object-level detection or tracking labels. Converting either setting into a second benchmark would require non-standard pseudo-labels and would not provide a controlled cross-dataset comparison. We therefore evaluate RoadOcc under one InfraOcc protocol and test architectural generality by transferring P/T/R to two temporal occupancy backbones under matched conditions. The benchmark contains 290 temporally continuous roadside sequences, with 215 used for training and 75 for evaluation. Each sequence spans approximately 10--24 seconds. Raw streams are captured at 10 Hz and dense occupancy is labeled at 2 Hz, giving the 0.5 s interval used by RoadOcc. Each keyframe contains four calibrated camera views and a semantic occupancy volume over \([-64, 64] \times [-64, 64] \times [-4.8, 1.6]\) m at 0.4 m resolution, or \(320 \times 320 \times 16\) voxels. Labels distinguish occupied, free, and unobserved space; unobserved voxels are excluded from supervision and evaluation. Occupancy construction separates persistent structure from transient objects. A semantic static scaffold is accumulated from registered vehicle-side LiDAR after dynamic-point removal. Dynamic geometry is reconstructed from infrastructure-side LiDAR using annotated object tracklets, box-guided alignment, and local registration. We therefore generate planar voxel-velocity targets from annotated dynamic boxes and their temporal tracklets. Raw box velocity is transformed to the fixed roadside frame and may be replaced by the adjacent-frame tracklet displacement when the latter is valid and consistent: replacement is allowed when the raw estimate is invalid, the speed difference is at most 10 m/s, or the speed ratio is at most two. Speeds below 0.8 m/s are treated as stationary, and abnormal magnitudes are clipped to 60 m/s. For track \(j\), let \(\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{rs}\leftarrow\mathrm{raw}}\) transform planar vectors from the annotation frame into the fixed roadside frame, and let \(\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{rs}}_{j,t}\) be its roadside-frame center. The two candidate velocities are \[ \tilde{\mathbf{v}}_{j,t} = \mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{rs}\leftarrow\mathrm{raw}} \mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{raw}}_{j,t}, \qquad \mathbf{d}_{j,t} = \frac{\mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{rs}}_{j,t+\Delta t} - \mathbf{c}^{\mathrm{rs}}_{j,t}}{\Delta t}, \qquad \Delta t = 0.5\ \mathrm{s}. \tag{11} \] We denote the selected candidate by \(\overline{\mathbf{v}}_{j,t}\). A valid tracklet displacement replaces the raw estimate when the raw estimate is invalid, when their speeds differ by at most 10 m/s, or when their speed ratio is at most two. The corrected velocity is rasterized over dynamic occupancy inside each box, whose vertical extent is expanded by a factor of 1.5 to absorb sparse boundary misalignment. Let \(\tilde{B}_{j,t}\) denote this expanded box. The native target assigned to a dynamic voxel is \[ \mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{gt}}_{t}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{0}, & \lVert \overline{\mathbf{v}}_{j,t} \rVert_2 < 0.8\ \mathrm{m/s}, \\[2mm] \mathrm{clip}_{60}(\overline{\mathbf{v}}_{j,t}), & \mathbf{x} \in \tilde{B}_{j,t} \cap \Omega^{\mathrm{dyn}}_{t}, \end{cases} \tag{12} \] where \(\mathrm{clip}_{60}\) limits the magnitude to 60 m/s. For candidates no faster than 2 m/s, a one-step (0.5 s) future-occupancy check compares zero-motion and transported same-class support. The check is applied only with at least eight support voxels; zero motion is selected when its score exceeds the transported score by at least 0.05. Finally, face-connected component repair propagates valid motion within the corresponding raw dynamic occupancy component, and targets are generated at native, 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 scales. Future occupancy is used only to construct offline supervision and evaluation targets. Neither future images nor future features are provided to RoadOcc at training or inference time. The P/T/R threshold \(\epsilon = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s}\) in the main paper is a numerical zero test applied after this construction; 14 the physical stationary decision in target generation uses the 0.8 m/s threshold above. Stating both thresholds separates label denoising from the executed P/T/R routing rule. ## B Evaluation Contract Aggregate occupancy is dominated by persistent structure and can therefore conceal missed or stale traffic participants. Standard protocols emphasize semantic and geometric IoU (Wang et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2023), whereas dynamic occupancy and flow require motion-aware diagnostics (Ma et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). Table A1 formalizes our evaluation contract on InfraOcc (Xiang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026). Dynamic and next-frame IoU measure semantic recovery at the current and flow-advected next-frame locations. Direct MAVE and DSR jointly measure motion accuracy and coverage. Static, geometric, and ray metrics serve as guardrails against degrading the fixed scene. This coupled evaluation prevents a model from appearing favorable merely by predicting fewer dynamic voxels or retaining stale evidence. Table A1: Metric and diagnostic scope.

Direct MAVE evaluates every valid GT dynamic voxel, whereas TP-MAVE is conditional on a correct semantic match and must therefore be interpreted with DSR. A valid routing improvement should increase dynamic IoU and DSR, decrease Direct MAVE, and preserve the static and geometric guardrails. Reporting these quantities together distinguishes improved semantic correspondence from a lower conditional error caused by reduced semantic support. For completeness, let \(\mathcal{D}\) be the set of evaluated dynamic classes, \(V_c = \{i : y_i = c\}\) the valid GT voxels of class \(c\), and \(V_c^{\mathrm{TP}} = \{i \in V_c : \hat{y}_i = c\}\). Classes without valid support are omitted from the corresponding class macro-average; \(\mathcal{D}'\) and \(\mathcal{D}''\) denote the supported classes for Direct and TP-MAVE, respectively. The two velocity metrics and semantic recall are \[ \mathrm{Direct\ MAVE} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}'|} \sum_{c \in \mathcal{D}'} \frac{1}{|V_c|} \sum_{i \in V_c} \|\hat{\mathbf{v}}_i - \mathbf{v}_i\|_2 . \tag{13} \] \[ \mathrm{TP\text{-}MAVE} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}''|} \sum_{c \in \mathcal{D}''} \frac{1}{|V_c^{\mathrm{TP}}|} \sum_{i \in V_c^{\mathrm{TP}}} \|\hat{\mathbf{v}}_i - \mathbf{v}_i\|_2 . \tag{14} \] Thus MAVE is class-macro while DSR is a micro recall over GT dynamic voxels. For next-frame dynamic IoU, centers of predicted current dynamic voxels are advanced by the predicted planar velocity for 0.5 s, transformed to the next roadside frame, and voxelized. Collisions use deterministic per-class majority assignment before class-macro IoU is computed against next-frame GT. This flow-advected diagnostic is distinct from the same-class radius-one hit score used only in the backwarp visualization. \[ \mathrm{DSR} = \frac{\sum_{c \in \mathcal{D}} |V_c^{\mathrm{TP}}|} {\sum_{c \in \mathcal{D}} |V_c|}. \tag{15} \] ## C Training Objectives RoadOcc groups its objectives by function so that each loss supervises one decision in the DCA–VVE–VDSF chain. Camera-depth supervision uses weight 0.5. Semantic occupancy is supervised from full resolution to 1/8 scale with weights [1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125]. The static, dynamic, and DCA-candidate auxiliaries each use weight 0.5. VVE receives class- and speed-balanced robust flow supervision at all four scales with weight 0.1. This coarse-to-fine supervision aligns every executed routing field with the resolution at which it controls temporal fusion. ### C.1 Candidate, Motion, and Routing Contract **DCA score.** Let \(\pi_{\text{cur}}\) and \(\pi_{\text{sta}}\) denote current and static-reference class probabilities, and let \(\mathcal{C}_{\text{sta}}^{+}\) contain the static classes together with the empty class. The executed change and dynamic scores are \[ \delta(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{\text{sta}}^{+}|} \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}_{\text{sta}}^{+}} |\pi_{\text{cur},c}(\mathbf{x}) - \pi_{\text{sta},c}(\mathbf{x})|, \tag{16} \] \[ p_{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}_{\text{dyn}}} \pi_{\text{cur},c}(\mathbf{x}), \tag{17} \] \[ c(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\max\{\delta(\mathbf{x}), p_{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x})\}} {\max_{\mathbf{y}} \max\{\delta(\mathbf{y}), p_{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{y})\} + 10^{-6}}. \tag{18} \] DCA ranks this normalized score. VDSF combines it with nonempty support before the fixed top-\(K\) selection. For an anchor \(\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{x}, z_r)\), \(c(\mathbf{r})\) is the score of the corresponding voxel-height bin and is shared across cameras before visibility masking. Let \(d_{n,r}\) be its projected depth, \(\hat{d}_n\) the winning predicted depth bin, and \(\Delta_d = 1\text{ m}\) the bin width. The executed depth-consistency factor is \[ \beta_{n,r} = \exp\left[ -\frac{\sigma^2}{2} \min_{\xi \in \{-\Delta_d,+\Delta_d\}} \left| d_{n,r} - (\hat{d}_n + \xi) \right|^2 \right], \qquad \sigma = 2. \tag{19} \] Deformable-attention weights are first softmax-normalized over sampled points, then multiplied by \(\beta\). They are not renormalized afterward; camera outputs are averaged over cameras retaining at least one visible anchor. 16 Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027 **VVE correspondence range.** At scale \(s\), the temporal branch forms a \(5 \times 5\) correlation volume with radius \(r = 2\). With a native 0.4 m grid and a 0.5 s interval, the explicit correlation evidence spans the following physical ranges. Each correlation operand is normalized to unit \(\ell_2\) norm with \(\epsilon = 10^{-6}\). The resulting volume has 25 channels and is concatenated with current and historical BEV embeddings, processed by two \(3 \times 3\) convolution blocks, and decoded as a two-dimensional velocity residual in m/s. The window bounds only the explicit matching evidence. The coarse velocity is added to each finer prediction and the final continuous residual is not clipped, so it does not impose a hard bound on predicted speed. The GT-flow study in the main paper isolates the value of transport addresses across speed ranges. In the temporal blend, the history branch receives weight \(0.5\mathbf{1}_{\text{hist}} \max_z p_{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{x}, z)\); this is current dynamic support gated by history validity, rather than a calibrated measure of historic correspondence.

**Native P/T/R target.** For a current dynamic voxel, the Transport source is \[ \mathbf{x}_{\text{src}} = \operatorname{round}\left(\mathbf{x} - \frac{\Delta t\, v_t(\mathbf{x})}{0.4\text{ m}}\right), \qquad \Delta t = 0.5\text{ s}. \tag{20} \] Persist tests the rigid address and Transport tests \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{src}}\). Support means that the nearest previous GT contains the same semantic class at the same height within a \(3 \times 3\) XY neighborhood (\(L_\infty\) radius one). Support is Boolean: one or more matching voxels suffice, with no instance-level tie-breaking. Out-of-grid or unsupported candidates are assigned Refresh rather than removed. The target follows InfraOcc’s voxel-level semantic supervision and therefore tests class-consistent support without requiring instance identities. **Coarse-to-fine FIFO routing.** At each decoder scale, the shared controller independently projects the current feature and nearest rigidly aligned history to eight channels. It adds eight-channel projections of the detached VVE flow (normalized by 10 m/s) and the detached, upsampled coarse P/T/R distribution, then applies a \(3 \times 3 \times 3\) refinement and a three-logit classifier. A lightweight native head upsamples the \(1/2\) context and combines it with native flow and the finest P/T/R distribution to produce the full-resolution endpoint. Each execution-scale distribution is shared across valid FIFO slots; slot age and cached VVE fields define source-consistent inverse-trajectory Transport addresses. Routed slots are concatenated before the fusion MLP. Invalid slots are masked, and every scene boundary clears all stage-local queues. Fusion uses the soft distribution; argmax is reserved for diagnostics. ## D Capacity and Efficiency Context Table A3 reports parameters, end-to-end latency, and occupancy accuracy for reproduced local configurations. ## F Implementation and Scope The production configuration uses four cameras, a ResNet-50 backbone, three decoder stages, a 0.4 m voxel grid, and a 0.5 s sampling interval. Models are optimized with AdamW for 24 epochs. Controlled variants share the same initialization policy, optimizer, schedule, scene-boundary queue reset, and InfraOcc evaluator. Only the designated factor is changed. P/T/R operates on semantic voxel support, matching the InfraOcc label space. Nearby same-class objects can share support within the local radius; when history has no supported source, Refresh uses the current-frame feature. The route target therefore supervises semantic evidence admissibility rather than instance identity. We report dynamic IoU, Direct MAVE, and DSR jointly so that semantic recovery, motion error, and support coverage remain visible beyond the GT-conditioned route diagnostic. 19
